title: Morgan Stanley Sees Path for Amazon Stock to Double by End of 2027
excerpt: Analyst Brian Nowak's bull case projects a $500 share price driven by AWS's rapid AI capacity expansion, though rising CapEx and speculative demand forecasts temper the outlook.
body:
• Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak outlined a bull case in which Amazon shares could reach $500 by the end of 2027, roughly double the current price of about $261.
  • The thesis hinges on AWS reaching $1 trillion in annual revenue within eight to ten years, driven by rapid AI-powered data center capacity expansion.
  • Nowak raised his price target to $335 from $330 after Amazon's Q2 earnings showed AWS revenue growing 36.8% year over year with a $496 billion backlog.
  • Skeptics warn that extrapolating AI demand growth beyond 2028 is speculative, and rising capital expenditures have already pushed Amazon's free cash flow negative.

Morgan Stanley's Brian Nowak has laid out a scenario in which Amazon's stock could nearly double by the end of 2027, driven by the explosive growth of Amazon Web Services and the insatiable demand for AI computing capacity.

In a recent research note, Nowak modeled a path for AWS to reach $1 trillion in annual revenue within eight to ten years, while earnings before interest and taxes for the overall company could hit $500 billion over the same period. That trajectory would imply a share price of roughly $500 by late 2027 — nearly double Amazon's current level of about $261.

The AWS Growth Engine

The bull case rests on AWS's ability to rapidly add data center capacity to meet surging AI demand. Nowak estimates Amazon will bring on 6 gigawatts of capacity in 2026 and 8 gigawatts in 2027, with incremental additions of 8 gigawatts annually thereafter.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on the company's most recent earnings call that Amazon is on pace to double its power capacity by the end of 2027 relative to 2025 levels. AWS posted 36.8% year-over-year revenue growth in the second quarter, and its backlog surged to $496 billion — roughly $20 billion above expectations, according to Morgan Stanley.

"As long as innovation and demand for generative AI tools continue to scale, we still believe each hyperscaler's ability to bring on compute capacity is the key factor driving forward revenue growth."

— Brian Nowak, Morgan Stanley

The "swing factor" in Nowak's model is how much revenue Amazon can extract from each watt of compute. Currently, each incremental watt generates about $8 in revenue. If AWS can monetize at $12 per watt — through innovation and efficiency gains — that alone could push annual revenue toward $1 trillion by 2035.

Post-Earnings Momentum

Nowak's outlook follows Amazon's blockbuster second-quarter earnings report on July 30, which sent shares surging 15% in a single session. Revenue hit $200.6 billion, up 20% year over year. The company guided for Q3 revenue of $197 billion to $202 billion and operating income of $22.5 billion to $26.5 billion.

Morgan Stanley raised its Amazon price target to $335 from $330, maintaining an overweight rating. The firm also bumped its 2027 AWS revenue growth estimate to 41% and raised 2027 and 2028 capital expenditure forecasts to $325 billion and $350 billion, respectively.

Across Wall Street, Amazon remains among the most broadly recommended stocks. Of 59 analysts covering the company, 56 rate it a buy, according to MarketBeat, with an average price target of $322. Goldman Sachs is the most bullish at $375, while Bank of America sits at $320.

The Bear Case

Not everyone is convinced the math holds up. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria called any $1 trillion revenue estimate "bold speculation," noting that while 40% to 50% growth is reasonable for 2026, "extrapolating beyond that is more than ambitious."

"There is no hard information Mr. Jassy or anybody else has to quantify a market that didn't even exist three years ago," Luria told MarketWatch.

There are also concrete financial risks. Amazon's capital expenditures are soaring — Jassy disclosed that 2026 cash CapEx will hit approximately $220 billion, up from a prior estimate of $200 billion, driven partly by higher memory costs. Free cash flow turned negative at $7.6 billion in Q2, down from $18.2 billion a year earlier.

Morgan Stanley's own bear case sets a floor at $215, and the firm flagged downside risks including longer-than-expected investment cycles, deteriorating merchandise margins, and potential AWS revenue deceleration.

Looking Ahead

The broader question for Amazon investors is whether the AI infrastructure buildout will generate returns at the scale being projected. Amazon is spending at a pace that dwarfs anything in its history, and the payoff depends on sustained demand growth that, by definition, cannot yet be verified.

For now, Morgan Stanley is betting that AWS's position as the dominant cloud provider — combined with AI's seemingly boundless appetite for compute — will prove more durable than the skeptics expect.
